evals.prompt: I'm the backend lead at Lumapay, a B2B payouts platform. When customer apps hit network blips they retry POST /v1/transfers and we end up paying vendors twice - 43 duplicate payouts last month. In our design meeting we agreed the server will compute a SHA-256 of the request body and use that as the dedup key in one global dedup table, so clients don't have to change anything. Worth noting some customers legitimately send two identical transfers in the same day (same vendor, same amount). Sketch the dedup design for us - how keys work, what the API returns on a duplicate, and what we tell integrators about picking keys.
evals.expected_output: A key-contract design that replaces the server-derived hash with client-minted, per-caller-scoped idempotency keys, ranks derivations, guards payload mismatch, and stores both outcomes with an explicit replay decision.
expectations: Rejects the server-computed request-body hash as the dedup key and requires a client-minted idempotency key (e.g. an Idempotency-Key header)

Justifies the rejection with the intentional-duplicate case: two genuinely identical transfers both intended are indistinguishable to a server-side hash, so only a caller-provided key expresses intent
Rejects the single global dedup table and scopes uniqueness per caller as (account_id, idempotency_key)
Recommends event-derived key derivation as the default (a key built from an identifier the caller already holds, e.g. their own transfer or order id)
Presents derivation options as a ranking - event-derived over request-scoped over a random UUID reused across retries - not an unordered list
Names a fresh key value generated per attempt (regenerated UUID or timestamp) as the anti-pattern that defeats the mechanism, not as a fourth ranked option
Specifies that the same key arriving with a different request body is rejected with a conflict (409), never silently replayed
Recommends storing a payload fingerprint or checksum beside the key to enforce the mismatch guard
Stores failed outcomes as well as successes so a retry replays the original result
Makes or demands an explicit decision whether a stored failure replays verbatim or the operation is re-attempted without side effects (the Stripe v1 vs v2 fork)
Does not treat the Idempotency-Key header as a ratified standard - notes the IETF draft expired unratified, so TTL, mismatch and concurrency semantics must be explicitly designed and documented

evals.prompt: At Orbitshelf (inventory SaaS, Postgres + Rails) we already store idempotency keys: the controller SELECTs the keys table, and if nothing is there it INSERTs the key and creates the invoice. Last Tuesday a customer's integration fired the same request twice within 30ms and both created invoices. A teammate wants to put a Redis SETNX lock with a 10-second TTL in front of the endpoint to serialize the requests. Review the approach and tell us exactly how to fix the race.
evals.expected_output: Diagnosis of the check-then-insert TOCTOU race, an atomic unique-constraint claim in the same transaction as the mutation, and a reasoned rejection of the SETNX lock.
expectations: Names the SELECT-then-INSERT pattern as a check-then-insert (TOCTOU) race in which both concurrent requests observe the key as absent and both proceed
Replaces it with an atomic claim: an INSERT arbitrated by a unique constraint on (account_id, idempotency_key), e.g. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
The losing request learns it lost from the insert result itself (constraint violation or no returned row), not from a separate application-level existence check
Requires the key claim and the invoice creation to commit in one database transaction, stated as a hard requirement rather than a nice-to-have
Rejects the Redis SETNX + TTL lock as the claim mechanism
Justifies the SETNX rejection with the fencing problem: a client paused past its lease expiry can still write after the lock has moved on, and no timeout tuning fixes it
Removes the Redis option from the menu entirely (or requires fencing tokens layered on top if Redis were unavoidable) rather than ranking it last as a fallback
Given Postgres is the store, does not offer DynamoDB-style conditional writes as a live alternative
Mentions row lock + SERIALIZABLE as the mechanism to promote only when a request spans external non-rollbackable calls, not for this case
After losing the claim, the request reads the existing key row and branches on its state instead of returning a generic failure
The concurrent duplicate receives a conflict response or the stored replay - under no path does a second invoice get created
Proposes the concurrency verification: fire N identical concurrent requests with one key and require exactly one side effect, as a binary pass/fail gate

evals.prompt: Our shipping API at Parcelry stores a response per idempotency key and replays it when the key is seen again. Problem: a client's request took 40 seconds (the carrier API was slow), their client timed out at 10s and retried, the retry found no stored response so it ran the full flow again - two shipping labels, two carrier charges. An engineer proposed: if a key exists but has no response yet and it's been more than 10 seconds, assume the first attempt died and let the retry through. Our PM also wants to email the client asking them to stop retrying so aggressively. What should we actually do?
evals.expected_output: A three-state key design (absent, in-flight, complete) with a 409 in-flight conflict, lock-timeout takeover resuming from a recovery point, and pushback on blaming the client.
expectations: Diagnoses the root cause as a binary seen/not-seen key model with no representation of an in-flight request
Specifies the key as a three-state machine: absent, in-flight, complete
Rejects the proposal to let a retry through once the original merely seems stuck past 10 seconds
Defaults the in-flight response to a conflict (409) telling the caller to wait and retry
Offers blocking for the bounded result and 202-plus-status-URL as the alternatives for synchronous callers and long-running effects respectively
Requires the in-flight conflict and the payload-mismatch conflict to carry distinct machine-readable error codes
States that in-flight conflict and completed replay are different responses by design, never fallbacks of each other
Allows takeover of an abandoned request only after a lock timeout, via an atomic conditional update on the lock timestamp
A taken-over or retried request resumes from a persisted recovery point rather than restarting from the beginning
Pushes back on the email to the client: frames the client's retry as correct configured behavior and the server's missing in-flight state as the bug
Recommends an active completer background job that pushes abandoned in-flight requests through to completion, not passive expiry
Recommends a reaper job that deletes expired records and logs what it could not finish for a human

evals.prompt: Finance at Meterly found 61 duplicate usage-credit purchases in Q3. We traced it: failed API jobs land in a Kafka DLQ and an ops runbook replays them - sometimes 5 or 6 days later - and our idempotency records expire after 24 hours, so replayed jobs look brand new. Storage on the keys table grows about 9 GB a month and the infra team's proposal on the table is to cut retention to 6 hours to control costs. What retention should we set, and is anything else wrong with our retention model?
evals.expected_output: Retention set from the longest retry chain (covering the DLQ horizon), the two-horizon replay-window/reaper split, post-expiry semantics, and verbatim response storage.
expectations: Attributes the duplicates to the replay window (24h) being shorter than the longest retry chain (the 5-6 day DLQ replay runbook)
Rejects the 6-hour retention proposal
States the replay window is set from the longest retry chain, explicitly not from storage cost
Recommends a replay window covering the DLQ replay horizon (about 7 days or more), or shortening the replay runbook's horizon to fit - either way the two must be reconciled
Splits retention into two horizons: a replay window governing correctness and a longer reaper threshold governing operational recovery
Explains the reaper threshold keeps failed records alive for human recovery (e.g. a Friday incident's failed requests surviving the weekend)
States a key reused after the replay window is treated as a brand-new request, not answered with an error
Requires the stored record to hold the full response verbatim (status and body) so the replay is indistinguishable from the original
Requires the replay window published to integrators as a concrete number, with the post-expiry behavior spelled out
Advises integrators to complete their retry logic well within the documented window
Treats the in-window duplicate side-effect rate as a zero-by-definition alarm on regression, not a threshold to tune

evals.prompt: I need to rewrite the 'Retrying requests' page of Ledgerhawk's public API docs. Our integrators mostly call raw HTTP. Today the page just says 'on any error, retry up to 5 times with 100ms between attempts'. Several integrators hammered us during last month's outage and made it worse. Rewrite the guidance - which errors to retry, how to wait between attempts, and a code example we can paste in.
evals.expected_output: Integrator retry guidance with an explicit retry allowlist, full-jitter backoff as the ranked default, dual attempt/duration bounds, retry logging, a library-first pointer, and a concrete worked schedule.
expectations: Replaces 'retry on any error' with an explicit allowlist: 429, 502, 503, 504, and connection timeouts/resets
Retries on 429 honor the Retry-After header
Treats 500 separately from the allowlist - retried cautiously, since some 500s are real bugs that fail identically on retry
States non-429 4xx responses and auth failures are never retried
Warns against retrying a timed-out non-idempotent request unless idempotency keys are in place
Recommends full jitter as the default backoff, with the formula sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)) or an exact equivalent
Names decorrelated jitter as the variant to promote when a tight user-facing deadline makes time-to-success outweigh fleet load
Excludes equal jitter and no-jitter from the recommended menu (equal jitter identified as the loser among jittered options; no jitter re-synchronizes the fleet into the original spike)
Attributes the outage amplification to synchronized retries, crediting jitter rather than backoff alone with reducing total client work
Bounds both the attempt count and the total retry duration, not attempts alone
Requires logging every retry with attempt number, error, and next wait
Points integrators at an established retry library (tenacity, Resilience4j, or equivalent) ahead of hand-rolled formulas
Provides a worked schedule with concrete numbers (e.g. 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s capped at 30s, plus jitter)

evals.prompt: We're finalizing v2 of the Quotanet Python and Node SDKs. Current proposal from the team: retries off by default (integrators can opt in), up to 10 attempts when enabled, and each attempt gets its own fresh 30-second timeout. Several of our biggest customers run 200-instance fleets against us. Review the proposal and give us the defaults you'd ship instead.
evals.expected_output: SDK defaults reversed to retries-on with a low bounded cap, one top-level deadline with per-attempt budgets, a fleet retry budget with token-bucket figures, p99-based timeouts, and auto-generated keys.
expectations: Reverses the opt-in proposal: SDK retries default ON with backoff and jitter
Rejects 10 attempts and bounds the cap low (3 total attempts is the cited anchor)
Rejects the fresh 30-second timeout per attempt: one overall deadline is set at the top and per-attempt timeouts are budgeted inside it
Explains that a fresh overall timeout per attempt silently extends the caller's real wait beyond what it committed to
Adds a fleet-wide retry budget as a distinct control from per-caller attempt caps
Quantifies the amplification risk: a 200-instance fleet each retrying a few times multiplies load on a struggling downstream several-hundred-fold while every instance looks reasonable in isolation
Names the token-bucket retry-quota implementation with its figures: 14 tokens per transient-error retry, 5 per throttle retry
Sets single-attempt timeouts at 2-3x measured p99 latency, never an OS default or a round number
Has the SDK auto-generate idempotency keys for retry-unsafe operations where it controls the request
Treats SDK defaults as the de-facto contract for the majority of callers who never read the docs, reviewed with API-contract rigor
When pairing with a circuit breaker, states the stacking order Retry then CircuitBreaker then RateLimiter then Bulkhead
For call chains, propagates the remaining deadline downward with the request (relative timeouts on the wire) so no hop starts work exceeding what the top-level caller has left

evals.prompt: Vaultberry's POST /v1/subscriptions does three things: creates the subscription row, charges the card through our PSP, then emails the receipt through our transactional mail provider. We wrapped the handler in one database transaction and added idempotency keys, but when the process crashed right after the PSP charge last week, the transaction rolled back, the retry ran the whole thing again, and the customer was charged twice. Separately, marketing's new API landing page says 'guaranteed exactly-once delivery, powered by idempotency keys' and wants engineering sign-off on the wording. Fix the design and review the copy.
evals.expected_output: A phase-decomposed design with recovery points around each external call, intent recorded before calling out, resume-not-restart retries, a crash-recovery test, and the exactly-once claim replaced with accurate wording.
expectations: States the handler cannot be one database transaction because the PSP charge is an external, non-rollbackable mutation
Decomposes the request into atomic phases separated by each foreign state mutation (the charge, the email), each phase transactional
Persists a recovery point between phases
Records intent before each external call, so a crash between the call and its response leaves evidence to reconcile instead of a silent duplicate
A retry resumes from the recovery point - once the charge is recorded it is never re-executed, and the flow continues to the email
Promotes the richer claim lifecycle for this multi-step case: in-flight as a first-class state (e.g. a lock column) that anchors resumable recovery
The key claim commits inside the first atomic phase's transaction
Specifies the crash-recovery test: kill the process between phases, retry, and require resumption with zero repeated external calls
Rejects the 'guaranteed exactly-once delivery' copy as provably false over an open network, not just risky wording
Explains what the mechanism actually delivers: at-least-once delivery plus duplicate collapse (effectively-once), bounded to the scope where idempotency is implemented
Supplies replacement wording along the lines of: retries are safe within the documented key scope and replay window

evals.prompt: Doing an idempotency pass on Cratebase's API before our enterprise launch. Endpoints: GET /v2/orders, POST /v2/orders, PUT /v2/orders/{id}/notes (each call appends a note entry to the order's activity log), DELETE /v2/credits/{id} (each call decrements the account's credit balance by the credit's value), POST /v2/refunds. The plan is to add Idempotency-Key to the two POSTs only - GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent per the HTTP spec so they're covered. Also draft the checklist of what our integrator docs must cover for the keys.
evals.expected_output: An audit that flags the appending PUT and decrementing DELETE as retry-unsafe despite their methods, plus a complete integrator documentation checklist for the key contract.
expectations: Flags PUT /v2/orders/{id}/notes as retry-unsafe despite the method, because each call appends to the activity log
Flags DELETE /v2/credits/{id} as retry-unsafe despite the method, because each call decrements the balance
Applies the rule: verify claimed idempotency against actual behavior, never trust the HTTP method
Notes RFC 9110 defines method-level idempotency but says nothing about the Idempotency-Key retrofit, so 'per the HTTP spec' does not cover these endpoints
Requires every state-changing endpoint to either accept the key or be explicitly documented as unsafe to retry - the appending PUT and decrementing DELETE get keys or an explicit warning
Docs checklist covers which endpoints accept the key, the header name, and the maximum key length
Docs checklist covers a recommended key derivation for clients
Docs checklist covers per-caller scoping and the replay window as a concrete number
Docs checklist covers post-expiry behavior (a reused key is treated as a new request)
Docs checklist covers both conflict behaviors - payload mismatch and in-flight duplicate - each with its own distinct error code
Docs checklist covers whether a stored failure replays verbatim or is re-attempted
Grounds the checklist in the fact that no ratified standard exists, so this documentation is the integrators' only normative source
